item.title: A Kerberos realm for the same people
item.description:
kerberos {
 realm = "EXAMPLE.ORG" # required, upper case
 keytab = "/etc/authnd/krb5.keytab" # required; must hold krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG
 listen = "127.0.0.1:88" # the default; UDP and TCP both
 lifetime = "10h" # the default, MIT's
}

A kerberos block makes authnd a KDC as well as a directory, throughgo-authn/kdc: the same people are issued tickets instead of only being looked up. It answers on UDP and TCP at the same address, requires encrypted-timestamp pre-authentication, and issuesaes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 tickets only. lifetime is a Go duration("10h", "90m"). The directory and the realm are equals: if either stops,the process stops, because a server that kept answering LDAP after its KDC died would look healthy to everything that does not speak Kerberos.

Refused at startup:

$ authnd check cases/realm-lower.hcl
authnd: kerberos: realm "example.org" is not upper case: clients uppercase the realm they derive from a domain, and would then ask for a realm this server does not answer for

and likewise a realm with no name, no keytab, an address that does not parse,a lifetime Go cannot read, and a kerberos block beside an mfa block(below).

The keytab

The keytab holds the key authnd signs its own tickets with —krbtgt/REALM@REALM — and one key per service it issues tickets to. It is the same file those services read. The krbtgt password is never typed again, so make it random. With MIT’s ktutil (package krb5-user on Debian and Ubuntu; this recipe is the onedocs/install.md gives, and was not run for these pages):

printf 'addent -password -p krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG -k 1 -e aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96\n%s\nwkt /tmp/krb5.keytab\nquit\n' \
 "$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)" | ktutil
sudo install -o root -g authnd -m 0640 /tmp/krb5.keytab /etc/authnd/krb5.keytab
rm /tmp/krb5.keytab

Add a service’s key the same way (-p nfs/files.example.org@EXAMPLE.ORG), and give that service the same key in its own keytab. On macOS, Heimdal’sktutil -k <file> add -r -p <principal> -V 1 -e aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 writes a random key without a password at all. Either way, read the keytab back before starting (klist -k with MIT, ktutil -k <file> list with Heimdal):

$ ktutil -k etc/authnd/krb5.keytab list
etc/authnd/krb5.keytab:
Vno Type Principal Aliases
1 aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG

A keytab without krbtgt/REALM is refused by check and at start; seecheck.The keytab is read once, at start: replacing it takes a restart.

Who can be issued a ticket

A KDC must decrypt the client’s pre-authentication with that person’s long-term key, so it needs the person’s password, not only a way to check one. check says who can and who cannot, with the reason:

$ authnd check realm
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
bob the configuration file an NT hash account, uidObject uid
dora a sqlite database a password account, uidObject uid
eli a sqlite database an NT hash account, uidObject uid
GROUP MEMBERS PUBLISHED AS
staff alice and bob groupOfNames
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
bob has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
dora has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
eli has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
group staff has no gidNumber: not a posixGroup, published as a groupOfNames (member DNs, no memberUid)
realm EXAMPLE.ORG on 127.0.0.1:18388 (udp and tcp), keytab etc/authnd/krb5.keytab
can be issued a ticket: alice and dora
CANNOT, whatever they type: bob and eli
a KDC must decrypt the pre-authentication with the person's key
bob and eli: an NT hash is only the RC4-HMAC key (RFC 4757), and this realm issues aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 alone, whose key is derived from the password itself
a bind carries a password
bob and eli cannot bind with a password: their sources hold only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against
no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served
the source has a ticket
a password (password, password_file, a SQL password column) yes
only an NT hash no: it is the RC4-HMAC key, and this realm issues AES only
only a password check (a users "ldap" directory behind this one) no: a source that only verifies a password cannot produce any key

For a directory behind this one, the last line of the realm part readsalice, bob, dora and eli: the source only verifies a password, so it cannot produce any key. That is structural rather than a matter of configuration,and finding it in check beats finding it from somebody whose kinit says their correct password is wrong.

kinit against it

A krb5.conf that names this KDC. ⛔ For MIT Kerberos the braces go on their own lines: its parser silently ignores a realm written on one line.

[libdefaults]
 default_realm = EXAMPLE.ORG
 dns_lookup_kdc = false
[realms]
 EXAMPLE.ORG = {
 kdc = 127.0.0.1:18388
 }

The same configuration served, and asked by macOS’s Heimdal kinit (--password-file reads the password from a file):

$ authnd --config realm
ldap on 127.0.0.1:3893, serving 4 people from the configuration file, then a sqlite database
realm EXAMPLE.ORG on 127.0.0.1:18388 (udp and tcp)
$ kinit --password-file=alice.pwin alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
$ klist
Credentials cache: FILE:ccache
Principal: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
Issued Expires Principal
Oct 26 12:42:50 2026 Oct 26 22:42:50 2026 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG
$ kinit --password-file=wrong.pwin alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
kinit: Password incorrect
$ kinit --password-file=bob.pwin bob@EXAMPLE.ORG
kinit: krb5_get_init_creds: Error from KDC: this realm holds no Kerberos key for that principal
$ kinit --password-file=dora.pwin zed@EXAMPLE.ORG
kinit: krb5_get_init_creds: Error from KDC: no such principal in this realm

The ticket lasts the default ten hours. bob typed the password their NT hash was computed from, and is still refused: the realm has no key for them. The KDC writes what it refused, with the Kerberos error code, to its output:

kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25)
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25)
kerberos: the timestamp does not decrypt (client etype 18, our key type 18): error decrypting: integrity verification failed
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication does not decrypt (code 24)
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: this realm holds no Kerberos key for that principal (code 9)
kerberos: refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: no such principal in this realm (code 6)

Pre-authentication required is the normal first round of a kinit: the client asks without pre-authentication and is told it is required, then asks again with it. alice’s successful kinit leaves only that line.

The realm says which names exist; the directory does not

An LDAP bind for a name nobody has is answered invalidCredentials, the same as a wrong password. The KDC answers no such principal in this realm (KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN, code 6), as Kerberos KDCs do. With akerberos block on an address others can reach, the list of names is therefore as guessable as it is from any KDC; listen defaults to loopback.

A password changed over LDAP

The KDC reads the same people the directory serves, so apassword changed over LDAP reaches the realm at once — the old one stops working for kinit the moment it stops working for a bind:

$ ldappasswd -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=alice,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y alice.pwin -t alice.pwin -T alice.new
$ kinit --password-file=alice.pwin alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
kinit: Password incorrect
$ kinit --password-file=alice.new alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
$

Not beside an mfa block 

$ authnd check cases/krb-mfa.hcl
authnd: kerberos and mfa together: the mfa block asks every bind for a password AND a code, and a kinit carries only the password -- this KDC has no second-factor pre-authentication, so a realm here would accept one factor where the mfa block demands two. Remove one of the blocks

RFC 4120’s encrypted-timestamp pre-authentication is keyed by the password alone. A second factor needs OTP pre-authentication (RFC 6560) inside FAST(RFC 6113), which this KDC does not implement. A realm here would hand out tickets on one factor to the people the mfa block says need two, and a ticket opens everything a bind does — so the choice is made closed: one or the other.

Ports

88 is privileged. Under the packaged unit, CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE covers it;a server run as an ordinary user wants a high port, as above, and akrb5.conf that names it.

item.title: krb5 — accepting a Kerberos ticket
item.description:
Is this Kerberos ticket good for this service? The acceptor half of Kerberos, and only that half: it holds a keytab, verifies the AP-REQ a client presents, answers with the AP-REP that proves the service is genuine, and then signs, verifies, seals and opens messages under the key that exchange established.

go get github.com/go-authn/krb5@v0.3.1

It never talks to a KDC and never issues a ticket, so whose tickets it accepts is somebody else’s decision. The issuing half iskdc, and this module does not depend on it — see why they are separate.Ticket decryption is gokrb5’s.

Why it exists

gokrb5 is a client library. It verifies an AP-REQ and cannot build the AP-REP that answers one. Every GSS-API client asks for mutual authentication — MIT’s own gss-client sets GSS_C_MUTUAL_FLAG with no way to turn it off — so a service that cannot produce an AP-REP completes no context at all. Building it is most of what this module adds.

Example 

package main

import (
 "errors"
 "fmt"
 "log"

 "github.com/go-authn/krb5"
 "github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8/keytab"
)

// establish is one GSS-API exchange: the client's AP-REQ in, the AP-REP out.
func establish(a *krb5.Acceptor, token []byte) (*krb5.Context, []byte, error) {
 ctx, apRep, err := a.Accept(token)
 if err != nil {
 return nil, nil, err // no context: refuse, never fall back to something weaker
 }
 // The client will not consider the context open until it has verified
 // apRep, so sending it back is not optional.
 log.Printf("%s (user %q, realm %q) until %s", ctx.Principal(), ctx.User(), ctx.Realm(), ctx.Expires())
 return ctx, apRep, nil
}

func main() {
 // In a service: krb5.Load("/etc/krb5.keytab", krb5.Principal("nfs/files.example.org")).
 // Here, an empty keytab, so the refusals can be seen.
 a := krb5.New(keytab.New(), krb5.Principal("nfs/files.example.org"))

 _, _, err := establish(a, []byte("not a token"))
 fmt.Println(errors.Is(err, krb5.ErrNotAToken), err)

 _, err = krb5.Load("/nonexistent/krb5.keytab")
 fmt.Println(errors.Is(err, krb5.ErrNoKeytab), err)
}
true krb5: not a GSS-API krb5 token: asn1: structure error: explicitly tagged member didn't match
true krb5: keytab "/nonexistent/krb5.keytab": open /nonexistent/krb5.keytab: no such file or directory

It needs github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8 for keytab.New, which krb5.New takes; krb5.Load reads a keytab from a path instead.

After Accept, a *Context says who: Principal() (alice@EXAMPLE.ORG), orUser() and Realm() apart. Mapping a principal to a local account is the caller’s policy: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG and alice@PARTNER.ORG both answer to“alice”. Expires() is when the ticket behind it ends, past which a server holding a long-lived connection should stop honouring it. MIC/VerifyMIC and Wrap/Unwrap sign; Seal/Unseal add confidentiality (sec=krb5p).A Context is not safe for concurrent use; an Acceptor is.

What it refuses, and why

A ticket this service will not accept — wrong service, wrong key,expired, replayed, a clock beyond ClockSkew (five minutes by default, MIT’s too) — is ErrRejected. Bytes that are not a GSS-API krb5 token areErrNotAToken, and a token that is not an AP-REQ is ErrNotAPReq. The errors are deliberately coarse: a client learns that its ticket was refused, never which check refused it. An error means no context, and the returned token is empty.

A principal the acceptor does not answer for. Withkrb5.Principal("nfs/files.example.org"), a keytab holding several services answers for that one only.

A message whose signature does not match is ErrBadMIC, whichever of the length, the header, the sequence or the checksum disagreed. The acceptor signs with key usage 23 and verifies with 25, so a token this server produced cannot be replayed back at it as though the client had signed it.

A sealed token given to Unwrap is ErrSealed, distinct from a bad signature: a caller reading an integrity-only token must not be handed ciphertext that reads like a message. An unsealed token given to Unseal is ErrNotSealed: a protocol that promised confidentiality is not handed something that crossed the wire in the clear.

It asserts no acceptor subkey: the context key is the subkey the initiator put in its authenticator, or the ticket’s session key when it sent none(RFC 4121 §4.3).

A keytab is a secret at rest

Its path may come from a configuration file or from KRB5_KTNAME; the key inside it must never be logged, printed, or carried in an environment variable.

What it is checked against

A real MIT KDC and MIT’s own gss-client, against this package standing in for gss-server. test/kdc.sh builds a throwaway realm on loopback,unprivileged; the CI gets MIT Kerberos through pkgx (Ubuntu’s packages do not ship gss-client). The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane set KRB5_REQUIRE_JUDGE=1, so a missing fixture fails. A further step runs TestMITClientAgainstThisAcceptor and fails unless the log saysauthenticated as alice@ — a green lane whose judge silently stopped running is not accepted. TestMITClientSealed does the same with confidentiality on.

The macOS, Windows and cross-architecture lanes have no realm, and there the judge skips. The coverage lane’s floor is 90%.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/krb5@v0.3.1

item.title: kdc — issuing Kerberos tickets from a directory
item.description:
How does a realm issue tickets from a directory? AS-REQ and TGS-REQ, over UDP and TCP, with encrypted-timestamp pre-authentication required, for the people a directory knows and the services a keytab holds. It runs underauthnd.

go get github.com/go-authn/kdc@v0.4.3

At v0.4.3 its go.mod requires at least go-authn/directory v0.12.0 and gokrb5 v8.4.4: minimums, so a program that requires directory v0.14.0, the version these pages describe, builds with v0.15.0, as authnd v0.12.3 does. The accepting half is krb5, and a service that only verifies tickets needs this module not at all.

Not implemented: cross-realm referrals, PKINIT, FAST, renewable or postdated tickets, and any kadmin protocol. Keys come from the directory and from a keytab, and change where they live.

Only a source holding the password can back a realm

A KDC must decrypt the client’s pre-authentication with that person’s long-term key, so a directory.Verifier — a bind against somebody else’s LDAP, a hash comparison — cannot serve, however well it answers is this the right password. A person whose source holds no password is answeredKDC_ERR_NULL_KEY (null key), never the code a wrong password gets, so it reads as a configuration to fix rather than a password to retype.

Example

A realm in memory, on loopback:

package main

import (
 "crypto/rand"
 "fmt"
 "log"
 "net"
 "time"

 "github.com/go-authn/directory"
 "github.com/go-authn/kdc"
 "github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8/iana/etypeID"
 "github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8/keytab"
)

func main() {
 // People: a source that holds PASSWORDS. A verifier cannot back a realm.
 people := &directory.Static{Name: "the configuration file", People: []*directory.Identity{
 directory.NewIdentity("alice", directory.WithPassword("correct horse battery staple")),
 }}

 // Services: the realm's own krbtgt key, and one per service.
 kt := keytab.New()
 for _, p := range []string{"krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG", "nfs/files.example.org"} {
 if err := kt.AddEntry(p, "EXAMPLE.ORG", rand.Text(), time.Now(), 1, etypeID.AES256_CTS_HMAC_SHA1_96); err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 }

 // A keytab without krbtgt/REALM is refused before anything listens.
 _, err := kdc.New(kdc.Config{Realm: "OTHER.ORG", People: people, Services: kt})
 fmt.Println(err)

 srv, err := kdc.New(kdc.Config{
 Realm: "EXAMPLE.ORG",
 People: people,
 Services: kt,
 Logf: log.Printf, // why each request was refused; never a key
 })
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 pc, err := net.ListenPacket("udp", "127.0.0.1:18088")
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:18088")
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 go srv.ServeTCP(ln)
 fmt.Println("EXAMPLE.ORG answers on", pc.LocalAddr())
 log.Fatal(srv.ServeUDP(pc))
}

With a krb5.conf naming kdc = tcp/127.0.0.1:18088 for EXAMPLE.ORG, the Heimdal kinit that macOS ships (1.5.1) gets a ticket-granting ticket, withKRB5_CONFIG=krb5.conf and KRB5CCNAME=FILE:cc:

$ kinit --password-file=STDIN alice@EXAMPLE.ORG < alice.pw
$ klist
Credentials cache: FILE:cc
Principal: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
Issued Expires Principal
Oct 26 12:34:16 2026 Oct 26 22:34:16 2026 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG
$ kinit --password-file=STDIN alice@EXAMPLE.ORG < bad.pw
kinit: Password incorrect
$ kinit --password-file=STDIN bob@EXAMPLE.ORG < alice.pw
kinit: krb5_get_init_creds: Error from KDC: no such principal in this realm
$ kgetcred nfs/files.example.org@EXAMPLE.ORG
$ klist
Credentials cache: FILE:cc
Principal: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
Issued Expires Principal
Oct 26 12:34:16 2026 Oct 26 22:34:16 2026 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG
Oct 26 12:34:16 2026 Oct 26 22:34:16 2026 nfs/files.example.org@EXAMPLE.ORG

The ten hours are Config.Lifetime’s default, and the service ticket ends with the ticket-granting ticket it was bought with. The KDC said why it refused each request, in its own log:

kdc: the keytab has no krbtgt key for this realm: matching key not found in keytab. Looking for "krbtgt/OTHER.ORG" realm: OTHER.ORG kvno: 0 etype: 18
EXAMPLE.ORG answers on 127.0.0.1:18088
2026/10/26 12:34:16 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25)
2026/10/26 12:34:16 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25)
2026/10/26 12:34:16 the timestamp does not decrypt (client etype 18, our key type 18): error decrypting: integrity verification failed
2026/10/26 12:34:16 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication does not decrypt (code 24)
2026/10/26 12:34:16 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: no such principal in this realm (code 6)

The first refusal of each exchange is the protocol working: the KRB-ERROR that demands pre-authentication carries an ETYPE-INFO2 hint naming the etype and the salt, and the client tries again with a timestamp.

Before v0.4.2, a till of 19700101000000Z got a ticket that had already expired

RFC 4120 §5.4.1: a till of 19700101000000Z asks for the maximum end time the KDC’s policy permits. Heimdal’s kgetcred sends exactly that. v0.4.1 tested only for Go’s zero time, so it took the Unix epoch for a real end and issued a service ticket that klist showed as >>>Expired<<<; MIT’s kvno,the CI’s judge, sends a real till and never met the case. v0.4.2 issues the longest ticket allowed, as above, and answers a till that has already passed with KDC_ERR_NEVER_VALID instead of a ticket expired on arrival(go-authn/kdc#19).

What it refuses, and why

At configuration (New): no realm (ErrNoRealm), no directory(ErrNoPeople), no keytab (ErrNoServices), or a keytab withoutkrbtgt/REALM@REALM (ErrNoTGTKey) — rather than starting and failing at the first kinit, where the error reaches a person who cannot fix it.

At the AS: a request without pre-authentication is answered with the demand for it, and the person’s key is not derived until there is a timestamp to check, so a spoofed UDP packet naming a real principal costs no key derivation. A wrong password, a timestamp under another etype and one from an hour ago are all answered KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED, the code a wrong password gets; the error text names the reason, and so does Logf. A service asking for a TGT of its own is refused: services authenticate from a keytab.

One encryption type. Tickets and keys are aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 (etype 18) only. A request whose etype list lacks 18 is answeredKDC_ERR_ETYPE_NOSUPP before anybody is looked up. With Logf set, the log records both etypes, so an operator can tell a mismatched cipher from a mistyped password.

At the TGS (RFC 4120 §3.3.2), a ticket is issued only when:

  • the ticket presented is a TGT of this realm, decrypted under thekrbtgt/REALM key the KDC names — not under the key of whatever service the ticket claims (KRB_AP_ERR_NOT_US);
  • the authenticator decrypts under its session key, within MaxSkew;
  • its checksum is over this request’s body, as the bytes arrived, keyed with the session key (KRB_AP_ERR_INAPP_CKSUM when missing or unkeyed,KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED when wrong);
  • the TGT is not past its end (KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_EXPIRED), not before its start and not flagged invalid (KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_NYV), with no skew allowed: this KDC’s clock wrote those times;
  • the client is of this realm and still in the directory(KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN).

Lifetimes. Config.Lifetime caps a ticket, ten hours when zero; a client asking for less gets less, and a ticket bought with a TGT ends no later than that TGT, so asking for krbtgt again cannot stretch a credential.

What an unauthenticated peer can hold: a TCP message, its length included,must arrive within 30 seconds; at most 256 TCP connections are served at once,and at most 64 datagrams are answered at once — one more is dropped, and the client resends or falls back to TCP.

What it is checked against

MIT’s own kinit and kvno, through pkgx, against a realm built in Go —no MIT KDC is involved, only the client is borrowed.TestMITClientGetsATGTAndAServiceTicket gets a TGT and a service ticket and checks the key version kvno reports. The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane set KDC_REQUIRE_JUDGE=1, and a further step fails unless the log says were served by this realm. The tests also pin the refusals a real client never triggers: a timestamp under the wrong key, one from an hour ago, a three-byte cipher, a service asked for straight from an AS-REQ, a forged service ticket at the TGS, and a realm backed by a verifier.The coverage lane’s floor is 80%.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/kdc@v0.4.3
